captions.instagram:
How does wall paint work?

A coat of wall paint is thinner than a hair, yet it hides a black wall. Watch millions of soft plastic balls squash into one film, follow photons lost in a maze of titanium dioxide, tint a white base, and find out why damp walls blister.

→ Wall paint is a liquid that becomes a solid skin: pigment, binder, water and a few per cent of additives.
→ On the wall it is the top of a stack: plaster, putty, primer and two coats, together as thin as a sheet of paper.
→ As emulsion paint dries, water leaves and millions of soft plastic balls crowd together.
→ The balls squash into a honeycomb and fuse into one film: touch dry within the hour, fully hard in a week or two.
→ White paint hides by scattering: photons bounce from grain to grain and stumble back out before they reach the wall.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/wallpaintclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does wall paint work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A coat of wall paint is thinner than a hair, yet it hides a black wall. Watch millions of soft plastic balls squash into one film, follow photons lost in a maze of titanium dioxide, tint a white base, and find out why damp walls blister.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/wallpaintclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/wallpaintclear

In this video:
• A liquid that becomes a skin. Paint is four things: pigment (the powder you see), binder (the glue that becomes the film), a carrier that leaves (water or solvent) and a few per cent of additives.
• Drying is three steps, not one. Water evaporates and the balls crowd until they touch.
• White hides by scattering. White pigment absorbs almost nothing.
• Colour subtracts, roughness dulls. Coloured pigments take wavelengths away: iron oxides soak up blue, phthalocyanine blue soaks up red, carbon black takes everything.
• Thick, thin, thick again. Paint is shear-thinning: about 80 Pa·s at rest, so pigment barely sinks, and hundreds of times thinner under the brush.
• Most failures are water, and the label matters. Blisters and peeling are water trapped behind a film that cannot pass it; the white bloom on monsoon walls is salt left by evaporating water; algae needs a surface that stays damp.
